name: Tsotsil
confidence_why: Laughlin 1975, Haviland 1981 and Aissen 2017 all describe Zinacantán Tsotsil with two prominences, a stronger one on the last syllable of the phrase, which a word said alone carries and which Laughlin 1975 and Polian 2024 call Tsotsil's final stress, and a weaker one on the first syllable of the root in connected speech, so whether word stress is final or root-initial depends on which prominence one counts as the word's, while the type (fixed, non-contrastive) is not in doubt outside the tonal Carranza dialect described by Polian 2024.
catalog_quote: Descriptions of Z Tsotsil characterize prosodic prominence at two levels – the word and the phrase. At the word level, stress falls on the initial syllable of the root; at the phrase level, it falls on the final syllable of the ιP (Laughlin 1975,23; Haviland 1981,14) (stress being predictable, it is not marked in the orthography).

new_statements.quote: Fuera del yucateco, uspanteko y mocho’, que han desarrollado tonos léxicos, las lenguas mayas, incluyendo el tseltal y tsotsil en general, no presentan prosodia contrastiva a nivel de palabra: ni acento tónico contrastivo como el del español, ni tonos (Bennett 2016; England & Baird 2017). En Carranza, las palabras se distinguen según el tono de su sílaba inicial, mientras que las sílabas siguientes reciben un tono predecible, con la excepción de ciertos sufijos. [...] El tsotsil de Carranza califica entonces como una lengua tonal: por definición, un acento tónico como el del español no permite distinguir pares de monosílabos (Hyman 2006).
new_statements.translation: Apart from Yucatec, Uspantek and Mocho', which have developed lexical tones, the Mayan languages, including Tseltal and Tsotsil in general, do not show contrastive prosody at the word level: neither a contrastive stress accent like that of Spanish, nor tones (Bennett 2016; England & Baird 2017). In Carranza, words are distinguished by the tone of their initial syllable, while the following syllables receive a predictable tone, with the exception of certain suffixes. [...] Carranza Tsotsil therefore qualifies as a tonal language: by definition, a stress accent like that of Spanish cannot distinguish pairs of monosyllables (Hyman 2006).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed: final syllable (non-contrastive) stress for Tsotsil at large: the paper says Tsotsil in general has no contrastive word-level prosody, and its one placement remark (p. 40) is final accentuation in Chamula Tsotsil, which agrees with the catalog. For the Carranza (San Bartolo) dialect it contradicts a stress analysis altogether: that variety has lexical H/L tone on the initial syllable, so the fixed: final syllable rule does not describe it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Tsotsil in general (and Tseltal): no contrastive word-level prosody, i.e. stress is not contrastive and there is no tone. For the Venustiano Carranza (San Bartolo) dialect specifically: a lexical high/low tone contrast on the initial syllable of the word (minimal pairs ólìl 'hijo' vs òlíl 'mitad', múy vs mùy), later syllables predictable; the author explicitly rejects an analysis in terms of stress accent because monosyllables contrast. Low initial tone historically comes from a lost *h in V_C (*CVhC). Elsewhere (p. 40) the author refers in passing to 'la acentuación final de tsotsil tanto en español como en tsotsil de Chamula' (final accentuation of the word 'tsotsil' in Chamula Tsotsil).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none stated; p. 26 fn. 6: in Carranza the phrase-final syllable is written without tone because 'la prosodia frasal remplaza al tono subyacente' (phrasal prosody replaces the underlying tone in the last syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Certain suffixes carry unpredictable tone; high-tone syllables are also longer and more intense; a full acoustic account is deferred to Polian & López Mendoza (in press).
new_statements.identity_note: Polian 2024 describes the Venustiano Carranza (San Bartolo) dialect, a divergent southern variety locally called 'tseltal' but shown to be Tsotsil; it alone has lexical tone. The Haviland page describes Zinacantán Tzotzil (speaker Juan Pérez Pérez of Nabenchauk). Cowan 1969 is the Huixtán dialect (not opened). Laughlin 1975 (earlier reading) is Zinacantán. Polian's passing remark on final accentuation concerns Chamula Tsotsil.

new_statements.quote: The primary accent of a word in Tzotzil falls on the first syllable of the root; there is also an even stronger accent that accompanies the last syllable of a phrase or sentence (it can consists of a single word, pronounced in isolation, or of words uttered in the same breath). [...] Here the symbol | represent word, and the symbol || represents phrasal accent, which is even more emphatic. It is clear that particles are not accented unless they are in final position.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level primary accent on the first syllable of the root (prefixes such as the possessive/readers j- do not carry it: jv|abaj||om 'musician'); a stronger phrasal accent on the last syllable of the phrase or sentence, which a word pronounced in isolation also receives; particles are unaccented unless phrase-final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Two levels are distinguished: word accent (root-initial) and a stronger phrase-final accent; no further secondary stress described.
new_statements.exceptions: Particles are not accented unless they are in final position.

readall_conflicts: The catalog records fixed: final syllable stress (StressTyp2). (1) Haviland's on-line Zinacantán Tzotzil pronunciation page says word-level primary accent falls on the first syllable of the root and that the final prominence is a stronger phrasal accent on the last syllable of the phrase (which a word in isolation receives); this is a different word-level placement (root-initial) from the catalog's final, though the two agree on what is heard on an isolated word. Laughlin 1975 p. 23 (opened in the earlier reading, file) states the same two-level picture in the catalog's terms: final stress on single words in isolation, with exceptions (affective verbs in -luh, 1pl exclusive suffixes, two-syllable reduplicated stems), and root-vowel plus phrase-end stress in normal speech. (2) Polian 2024 says Tsotsil and Tseltal in general have no contrastive word-level prosody (neither contrastive stress nor tone), which is compatible with a predictable fixed rule, and mentions final accentuation in Chamula Tsotsil; but the Venustiano Carranza (San Bartolo) dialect has developed lexical H/L tone on the initial syllable and Polian explicitly rejects a stress analysis for it. Bennett 2016 (held by the project from the earlier reading) records the counter-view of Herrera Zendejas 2014 that the San Bartolo pitch differences reduce to word-final stress plus laryngeal effects, so the tonal status of Carranza is itself disputed.
